item.title: Your Agent's Memory Store Gets Stale — Dreams Run an Async Cleanup Pass Over Past Sessions and Hand You a Reorganized Store to Review
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Dreaming is an async API call that reads a memory store plus 1-100 past sessions, runs a dedup-and-synthesize pass, and returns a cleaned output store for you to review and swap in.
item.content:encoded:
**Dreaming is an async API call that takes a memory store + 1–100 past sessions, runs a dedup-and-synthesize pass, and returns a cleaned output store you review and swap in on your next session.**
Every session write is local and incremental: preferences, corrections, and task facts accumulate in a Claude Managed Agents memory store over time. After a few weeks you have duplicates, contradictions, and entries that no longer match the current work. You can prune manually — or you can let the model do it.
```python # Requires: anthropic-beta: managed-agents-2026-04-01,dreaming-2026-04-21 dream = client.beta.dreams.create( inputs=[ {"type": "memory_store", "memory_store_id": store_id}, {"type": "sessions", "session_ids": [session_a, session_b, session_c]}, ], model="claude-opus-4-8", instructions="Focus on coding-style preferences; ignore one-off debugging notes.", )
# Dreams run asynchronously — poll until complete while dream.status in ("pending", "running"): time.sleep(10) dream = client.beta.dreams.retrieve(dream.id)
# Use the output store in your next session output_store_id = next( o.memory_store_id for o in dream.outputs if o.type == "memory_store" ) session = client.beta.sessions.create( agent=agent_id, environment_id=env_id, resources=[{"type": "memory_store", "memory_store_id": output_store_id}], ) ```
The input store is **never modified**. You get a separate output store to inspect via the Memory Stores API or the Console before you decide whether to attach it to production agents.
**When to run it:** After 10+ sessions of activity on one agent, or when the agent starts acting on stale context. The `instructions` field steers what survives vs. what gets merged — useful when certain memory categories matter more than others ("ignore debugging notes from last quarter" keeps the store lean).
**Three limits:** 1. **Research preview — gated.** Dreams need the `dreaming-2026-04-21` beta header and a separate access request at `claude.com/form/claude-managed-agents`. If you're already using Managed Agents, apply separately for dream access. 2. **Cost scales with session count.** Billed at standard API token rates; start with 2–5 sessions to calibrate before running across your full history. 3. **Synthesis can introduce errors.** The reorganized store is Claude's interpretation of patterns — review it before attaching to a production agent. Inspect individual memories with the Memory Stores API; apply targeted corrections with `store.update()` before promoting.
**Sources:** [Dreams — Anthropic Platform Docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/dreams) · [Claude Managed Agents: Dreaming, Outcomes, Orchestration — Developers Digest](https://www.developersdigest.tech/blog/claude-managed-agents-dreaming-outcomes-multi-agent)

**Two separate October 5 announcements worth tracking: OpenAI's invisible text watermarking for EU compliance is live as an opt-in; Reflection AI previewed a large open-weight model targeting coding and agent workloads.**
**textGrain: watermarking AI-generated text.** From October 5, [OpenAI API customers globally can opt in](https://openai.com/index/text-watermarking/) to textGrain — an invisible statistical signal embedded in token sampling that flags AI-generated text. ChatGPT and Codex users in the EU will get it applied automatically in the coming weeks, under Article 50 of the EU AI Act (in force since August 2, 2026). A detector is available to researchers and qualified organizations on application; the SDK gains a `watermark` parameter on the Responses API.
One published limit: replacing 25% of the output's words with synonyms drops detection from 92% to 17%. The signal degrades with paraphrase, which is the same property that limits all statistical watermarking schemes.
**Why it matters:** If you build apps serving EU users via the OpenAI API and downstream that text, your provider's output is now signed with a detectable signal users can't see. As the EU Act enforcement ramps, expect other providers to follow with equivalent implementations.
**Reflection AI Beam.** [Reflection AI previewed Beam](https://reflection.ai/blog/introducing-beam), a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 501B total parameters and 23B active, trained on 23.8T tokens. Reflection claims it's competitive with larger open models like GLM-5.2 on coding and agentic tasks. The weights aren't out: the model is on a waitlist, with an Apache 2.0 release expected "later in October 2026." Independent benchmarks won't exist until the weights ship.
**Why it matters:** Another potential high-efficiency open-weight option for teams that self-host inference. Worth watching, but premature to plan around — the gap between a preview claim and what independent evals show on your task can be wide.

item.title: Your Agent Starts Fresh Every Session — LangGraph's Checkpointer and Store Fix Different Halves of That Problem
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: LangGraph's checkpointer tracks conversation within one thread; a Store persists user facts across threads. They work differently and you need both — here's the pattern and when to swap in production backends.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Build a LangGraph agent that maintains conversation history within a session (checkpointer) and user-specific facts across sessions (store), then swap the dev-only in-memory backends for production PostgreSQL without touching graph logic.
**Three takeaways:** 1. **Checkpointer ≠ store.** A checkpointer saves conversation within one `thread_id` — it resets when the thread changes. A store persists user-scoped facts across *any* thread. The most common LangGraph memory architecture mistake is using a checkpointer to solve a cross-session problem. 2. **Checkpointer is automatic; store requires explicit node code.** Compile with `checkpointer=` and LangGraph manages conversation history automatically. Store reads and writes belong in your node functions: `store.search()` before the model call to load context, `store.put()` after the response to save new facts. 3. **Swapping backends is one argument.** `InMemorySaver` → `SqliteSaver` or `PostgresSaver`; `InMemoryStore` → `PostgresStore`. Both take a connection string; your graph logic is unchanged.
**The pattern:**
```python from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite import SqliteSaver from langgraph.store.memory import InMemoryStore from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings
# Dev backends — replace with PostgresSaver/PostgresStore in production checkpointer = SqliteSaver.from_conn_string(":memory:") store = InMemoryStore( index={"embed": OpenAIEmbeddings(), "dims": 1536, "fields": ["memory"]} )
graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer, store=store)
# In a node: load relevant long-term memories before the model call def call_model(state, config, *, store): user_id = config["configurable"]["user_id"] memories = store.search( ("users", user_id, "facts"), query=state["messages"][-1].content ) # Inject memories into system prompt
# After a response: save new facts the user stated def save_facts(state, config, *, store): user_id = config["configurable"]["user_id"] store.put( ("users", user_id, "facts"), key="stack_preference", value={"memory": "Prefers TypeScript and Next.js for all new projects"} ) ```
**Three limits:** - `InMemoryStore` is session-only and not safe for concurrent writes — never use it in production. - Semantic search in the store adds an embedding call per node read; cache the embedding when you call the same store in a tight loop. - LangGraph does not auto-expire memories. Stale facts accumulate without a pruning strategy — plan for periodic cleanup (or use [LangMem's forgetting policies](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langmem/), which sit on top of the same store API).
**Resource:** [How to Add Memory in LangGraph AI Agents — YouTube full tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=59GB3tW2Kns) · [Official LangGraph memory docs](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/add-memory) · [LangMem](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langmem/)

item.title: Your API Hard-Codes a Thinking Budget — Adaptive Thinking Lets the Model Decide; Fable 5 and Mythos 5 Only Accept the New Form
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 don't accept budget_tokens at all — adaptive thinking is the only mode. Here's the migration pattern and when manual budgets still make sense on older models.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 don't accept `budget_tokens` at all — the only thinking mode is adaptive. If you're passing a manual budget today, migrate before you hit a model you can't use.**
Extended thinking on older models used an explicit token budget:
```python # ❌ Works on claude-3-7-sonnet, claude-opus-4.6; fails on Fable 5 / Mythos 5 response = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-4-6", max_tokens=16000, thinking={"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 8000}, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}] ) ```
Adaptive thinking replaces the explicit budget with model-driven reasoning:
```python # ✅ Works on Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Fable 5, Mythos 5 response = client.messages.create( model="claude-fable-5-1", max_tokens=16000, thinking={"type": "adaptive"}, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}] ) ```
The model decides when deep reasoning is worth the tokens and when it isn't. A classification prompt won't burn thinking tokens; a multi-step logic problem will reason deeply. Anthropic reports this outperforms a fixed budget on most benchmarks because the model can scale effort to actual difficulty.
## Reading the output
The response still includes a `thinking` content block when the model used extended reasoning — your parsing code doesn't change:
```python for block in response.content: if block.type == "thinking": print("Reasoning:", block.thinking[:200]) elif block.type == "text": print("Answer:", block.text) ```
## When manual budget_tokens is still the right choice
- **Older models** (claude-3-7-sonnet, claude-opus-4, claude-opus-4.6, claude-sonnet-4.6): manual budgets still work and give you a hard ceiling on thinking cost. - **Evaluation pipelines with strict cost caps**: when you're running thousands of classification calls and don't want any of them to surprise you with a 20,000-token thinking pass, a hard budget is your guardrail. - **Debugging**: forcing a minimum thinking budget (`budget_tokens: 8000`) reproduces reasoning traces reliably; adaptive mode may not trigger for trivial test prompts.
## The limit to know
Adaptive thinking gives you less cost predictability than a hard budget. Thinking tokens cost the same as input tokens on the same model — a complex prompt could trigger a long reasoning pass without warning. Monitor `usage.thinking_tokens` in your response objects and set `max_tokens` high enough to accommodate the worst case.
**Sources:** [Adaptive thinking — platform.claude.com](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/adaptive-thinking) · [Extended thinking — platform.claude.com](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking) · [Extended Thinking in Claude: When Deep Reasoning Pays For Itself — developersdigest.tech](https://www.developersdigest.tech/blog/extended-thinking-claude-production-guide) · [Claude Extended Thinking API: Cost & When to Use 2026 — apiscout.dev](https://apiscout.dev/guides/claude-api-extended-thinking-mode-2026)

item.title: Your Local Machine Is an Inference Server — Ollama Turns a Model Download Into an OpenAI-Compatible REST API in One Command
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Ollama wraps llama.cpp with a single CLI for pulling and running 7B+ models locally; your existing OpenAI SDK code connects by changing base_url to http://localhost:11434/v1.
item.content:encoded:
**Ollama wraps llama.cpp with a one-command CLI for pulling, running, and serving open-weight models; your existing OpenAI SDK code connects by changing `base_url` to `http://localhost:11434/v1`.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Pull and run Llama 3.2, Phi-3.5, Mistral, and Qwen locally with no API key or cloud dependency - Call your local model from Python code that already uses the OpenAI client — zero rewrite - Pick the right quantization level for your RAM budget (the [GGUF post from yesterday](https://cloudcodetree.com/ai-news/2026-10-04-07-gguf-quantization-q4-k-m-q8-local-model-selection) has the tradeoff table)
## Setup (macOS/Linux, under 5 min)
```bash curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh # Windows: download installer at ollama.com ollama pull llama3.2 # 2.0 GB, runs on 8 GB RAM ollama pull phi3.5 # 2.2 GB, strong at reasoning for its size ollama run llama3.2 # opens an interactive chat shell ```
## Your existing OpenAI code works unchanged
Ollama serves `/v1/chat/completions` on `localhost:11434`, matching the OpenAI API shape:
```python from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="ollama") response = client.chat.completions.create( model="llama3.2", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a Python decorator that logs execution time."}] ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ```
`api_key="ollama"` is a placeholder the SDK requires; Ollama ignores it.
## Useful CLI
```bash ollama list # all downloaded models ollama ps # what's currently loaded in GPU/CPU memory ollama show llama3.2 # metadata: family, parameters, context length, quantization ollama rm llama3.2 # delete model and reclaim disk space ```
## The limits that matter
**RAM is your wall.** 7B models need ~6 GB VRAM (or ~8 GB system RAM for CPU inference); 13B need ~10 GB; 70B need ~40 GB. Q4 quantization cuts those numbers roughly in half at some quality cost. Loading a model for the first time takes 5–30 seconds depending on disk speed; subsequent requests are fast.
**Disk adds up.** Models store in `~/.ollama/models/` — a few 7B downloads fill a laptop SSD. Run `ollama rm` to prune models you're done with.
**The `/v1/` compatibility layer has gaps.** Ollama's OpenAI-compatible endpoint does not support the Batch API, `o1`-style reasoning tokens, or fine-tuned model IDs. Tool use and structured output work on most models but behavior varies by model family.

item.title: Your Similarity Search Scans Every Vector — FAISS IVF Clusters First, HNSW Graphs It: Pick the One That Scales
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: FAISS is the in-process ANN library for similarity search without a DB server. IVF clusters at train time and searches a subset; HNSW builds a graph and needs no training. Both beat brute-force past 100K vectors.
item.content:encoded:
**FAISS is Meta's in-process ANN library for similarity search when you want no server. IVF clusters at train time and searches a subset of them; HNSW builds a navigable graph and needs no training. Both beat brute-force past 100K vectors.**
## What you'll be able to do after this:
Run approximate nearest-neighbor search over millions of vectors inside a Python process — no Postgres, no Chroma server, no Qdrant — and know when to hand off to a managed vector DB instead.
**Three things to take away:**
1. `IndexFlatL2` is exact brute-force: no training, always correct, but O(n) per query. Use it only for baselines and datasets under ~100K vectors. 2. `IndexIVFFlat` clusters vectors into `nlist` buckets at train time; at query time it searches only `nprobe` buckets. Fast, but recall drops if `nprobe` is too low. 3. `IndexHNSWFlat` builds a multi-layer proximity graph — no training required, high recall at high QPS, but uses 2–3× more RAM than IVF at millions of vectors.
## Walk-through
```bash pip install faiss-cpu sentence-transformers ```
```python import faiss import numpy as np from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
encoder = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2") docs = [ "Embeddings are dense vector representations of text", "FAISS indexes vectors for approximate nearest-neighbor search", "Chunking splits documents before embedding them", ] vecs = encoder.encode(docs).astype("float32") # FAISS requires float32 d = vecs.shape[1] # 384 for MiniLM
# --- IVF --- nlist = 2 # ~sqrt(N) in real data quantizer = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d) index_ivf = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(quantizer, d, nlist) index_ivf.train(vecs) # required: learns cluster centers index_ivf.add(vecs) index_ivf.nprobe = 1 # how many clusters to search
q = encoder.encode(["vector similarity"]).astype("float32") D, I = index_ivf.search(q, k=2) print([docs[i] for i in I[0]])
# --- HNSW --- m = 32 # edges per node (16–64) index_hnsw = faiss.IndexHNSWFlat(d, m) index_hnsw.add(vecs) # no training step D2, I2 = index_hnsw.search(q, k=2) print([docs[i] for i in I2[0]]) ```
## When to use which
| | IVF | HNSW | |---|---|---| | Training required | Yes | No | | Memory | Lower | 2–3× higher | | Recall tuning knob | `nlist` / `nprobe` | `efSearch` | | Best for | Large datasets, memory-constrained | High throughput, simpler ops |
**FAISS is in-memory only** — no persistence between restarts, no built-in delete (you rebuild or use `remove_ids` on an IDMap wrapper). For production workloads that need durability or deletes, use pgvector or ChromaDB as the store and optionally layer FAISS as a read-side cache.
**Primary resource:** [Pinecone FAISS series — vector indexes deep-dive](https://www.pinecone.io/learn/series/faiss/vector-indexes/) covers recall@k benchmarks at scale and IVF-PQ (adding product quantization to cut memory further).
**Sources:** [Pinecone FAISS tutorial](https://www.pinecone.io/learn/series/faiss/faiss-tutorial/) · [FAISS ANN explained — PyImageSearch 2026](https://pyimagesearch.com/2026/02/16/vector-search-with-faiss-approximate-nearest-neighbor-ann-explained/) · [FAISS Python API reference — GoLinuxCloud](https://www.golinuxcloud.com/faiss-python-api/)

item.title: Your Repetitive Claude Code Tasks Are Three Lines of Markdown — Custom Slash Commands Take $ARGUMENTS and Live in Git
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: A .claude/commands/ markdown file becomes a slash command; $ARGUMENTS injects what you type after the slash. Commit the folder and every teammate gets the same project commands on pull.
item.content:encoded:
**A `.claude/commands/<name>.md` file becomes `/name` in every Claude Code session; `$ARGUMENTS` injects whatever you type after it. Commit the folder to git and the whole team shares the same project vocabulary.**
Claude Code's built-in commands (`/compact`, `/doctor`, `/goal`) are useful, but your project has repetitive tasks the defaults don't cover: a PR review checklist, a migration format, a release note template. Custom commands solve that in three files.
## How it works
Drop a markdown file in `.claude/commands/`. The filename (without extension) becomes the slash command:
- `.claude/commands/review.md` → `/review` - `.claude/commands/migrate.md` → `/migrate`
`$ARGUMENTS` is replaced with everything you type after the command name:
```markdown <!-- .claude/commands/review.md --> Review $ARGUMENTS for correctness, security, and the conventions in CLAUDE.md. Run the project lint and tests against the changes before summarising. List any violations of CLAUDE.md rules explicitly — don't soften findings. ```
Then:
``` /review src/components/AuthWidget.tsx ```
Claude receives the full expanded prompt and runs your checklist — not a generic review.
## Sharing with the team
```bash git add .claude/commands/ git commit -m "chore: add shared slash commands" ```
Everyone who pulls gets the same commands with no setup. This is the most underused form of team-level Claude Code standardisation: your review protocol, migration rules, and release checklist live in the repo, not in a wiki entry nobody re-reads.
## YAML frontmatter to lock down the run
Commands now support frontmatter for tool restriction and model selection:
```markdown --- allowed_tools: [Read, Grep, Glob] model: claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 --- Audit $ARGUMENTS for any import that does not appear in package.json dependencies. ```
This turns the command into a sandboxed, cheap read-only check — useful for the kind of routine scan you don't want running Bash.
**Limit:** `$ARGUMENTS` is a flat string. For multi-parameter or structured input, a skill with defined argument slots gives you more control. Commands also run in your current session and inherit its full context — which is usually what you want, but can be surprising if you run them from a heavily loaded session.
**Sources:** [Custom slash commands — Claude Code Docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/features-overview) · [Claude Code Custom Slash Commands 2026 — DEV Community](https://dev.to/stacknotice/claude-code-custom-slash-commands-2026-automate-your-repetitive-workflows-2il2)

item.title: Your Local Model Tag Is a Quality Setting — GGUF Quantization Levels, When Q4_K_M Is Enough, and When Q8_0 Is Worth It
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: GGUF quantization maps model size to quality: Q4_K_M halves VRAM vs FP16 at 98.9% accuracy; Q8_0 recovers 99%+ at 2x the size. Pick based on task, not instinct.
item.content:encoded:
**GGUF quantization maps model size to quality: Q4_K_M is the practical default at ~98.9% of FP16 quality; Q8_0 recovers 99%+ at roughly double the file size. The tag on your model is a decision you're making by default.**
## What you'll be able to do after this: - Read a GGUF quantization tag and know what quality-memory tradeoff you accepted - Choose the right level for code generation, structured output, and retrieval tasks - Use `ollama show` and `ollama ps` to audit what's actually running
When you run `ollama pull llama3.3:8b`, Ollama silently downloads Q4_K_M — a 4-bit quantized checkpoint that's ~4.6 GB instead of ~15 GB at FP16. That default hides a decision you probably want to make consciously.
## Reading the tag
GGUF K-quants use mixed precision: different tensor groups get different bit widths, with the most sensitive layers kept at higher precision. The tag encodes the scheme:
| Tag | Avg bits | ~Size (8B model) | Quality vs FP16 | |---|---|---|---| | Q4_0 | 4.5 | ~4.1 GB | 97.8% | | Q4_K_M | 4.8 | ~4.6 GB | 98.9% | | Q5_K_M | 5.7 | ~5.3 GB | 99.3% | | Q6_K | 6.6 | ~6.1 GB | 99.6% | | Q8_0 | 8.0 | ~7.7 GB | 99.8% |
Source: Red Hat's 500,000-evaluation benchmark suite across instruction-following, summarization, and code tasks.
**Q4_K_M is the right default** for iteration, exploration, and general chat. The 0.1% quality gap vs Q8_0 is invisible on most prompts. Pick it when RAM is the binding constraint.
## When Q8_0 earns its extra 3 GB
- **Structured output** (JSON schema, strict formatting) — the extra precision holds format constraints more reliably; Q4 drift can produce a valid-looking JSON that fails schema validation - **Code generation** — particularly for complex multi-file edits or uncommon API surfaces where exact token choice matters - **Short, factual answers** — a 1–2 sentence response where the quality gradient can flip the meaning
## Checking and controlling what you run
```bash # See the quantization level, parameter count, and context length of any local model ollama show llama3.3:8b
# Show active model and live VRAM usage ollama ps
# Pull an explicit Q8_0 checkpoint ollama pull llama3.3:8b-instruct-q8_0
# Pull via explicit tag — Ollama's library page lists available tags per model ollama pull qwen3:8b-q5_k_m ```
**Limit:** quantization does not address model selection — a smaller model at Q8_0 can underperform a larger model at Q4_K_M. Tune quantization only after you've picked the right model for the task. Also: not every model on Ollama's library exposes the full quant range; some only publish Q4_K_M and Q8_0 checkpoints.
**Sources:** [GGUF Format: A Complete Guide — DataCamp](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/gguf-format-a-complete-guide) · [GGUF Quantization for Fast and Memory-Efficient Inference — kaitchup/Benjamin Marie](https://kaitchup.substack.com/p/gguf-quantization-for-fast-and-memory) · [Red Hat Q4_K_M vs Q8_0 500k evaluation — sitepoint.com](https://www.sitepoint.com/quantized-local-llms-4bit-vs-8bit-analysis/) · [llama.cpp quantize README — GitHub](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/quantize/README.md)

**Claude Code's Workflow tool generates a JavaScript orchestration script that fans out to dozens (or hundreds) of subagents, runs in the background, and returns structured results — while your session stays free to do other work.**
When a task outgrows one context window — a 50-file migration, a parallel audit across every API route, a multi-repo research sweep — ask Claude to "use a workflow" or include "ultracode" in your prompt. The runtime executes the script, not Claude's internal planner, so intermediate results never fill your context.
## The three building blocks
```js export const meta = { name: 'audit', description: 'Audit all routes' }
const SCHEMA = { type: 'object', properties: { findings: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } } } }
const results = await pipeline( routeFiles, file => agent(`Audit ${file} for OWASP Top 10`, { label: `audit:${file}`, schema: SCHEMA }) ) return { findings: results.flatMap(r => r.findings) } ```
- **`agent(prompt, opts)`** — spawns one subagent, returns its structured or text result - **`pipeline(items, item => ...)`** — one agent per item, no global barrier; items flow through independently as each finishes - **`parallel([() => agent(...), ...])`** — global barrier; all must finish before the next stage
Default to `pipeline()`. Use `parallel()` only when a later stage genuinely needs every prior result at once — for voting, merging, or deduplication across the full set.
## When a workflow beats plain subagents
With the Agent tool or subagents, Claude is the orchestrator — every result feeds back into one context window. That works for tasks up to roughly 10 independent units. A workflow moves the orchestration logic into JavaScript outside Claude's context, so 50 or 100 agents report their JSON results directly to the script. The script is resumable: re-invoke with `resumeFromRunId` and completed `agent()` calls return their cached results instantly — no re-running what already settled.
## One real limit
Workflows require explicit user opt-in ("use a workflow", "ultracode", or `/config`). Every subagent call bills your usage separately — a 50-agent run costs as much as 50 conversations. Calibrate on a small input list before scaling.

item.title: A Poisoned .git/config in a Zip File Runs Code in Seven AI Coding Agents Before Any Permission Prompt
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Manifold Security disclosed GitSpawn: 8 CVEs across 7 AI coding agents. A malicious .git/config triggers RCE via core.fsmonitor before any model-level permission prompt runs.
item.content:encoded:
**Manifold Security disclosed GitSpawn: a poisoned `.git/config` in a received zip file, shared folder, or USB stick triggers arbitrary code execution in seven AI coding agents when any background `git status` runs — before any permission prompt is shown.**
Git's `core.fsmonitor` config key accepts a shell command that git runs whenever it checks file state. A `.git/config` file that sets this key doesn't need a `git clone` to arrive — it can come via a zip, a mounted share, or a CI artifact. Open a project folder, an agent runs a routine `git status` in the background, and the payload executes as you, outside the sandbox.
**Patching status at disclosure:** - **Claude Code 2.1.196+**: patched — update to 2.1.289+ (latest) - **Codex CLI 0.152.1+, Cursor (latest), Goose 1.44.0+**: patched - **Hermes Agent, Qwen Code, Grok Build**: unpatched at time of writing
Eight CVEs across the seven affected agents.
**Why it matters:** This bypasses the agent permission model. Watching what the agent does and denying suspicious commands doesn't help — the payload runs before the model receives any request. The attack surface is any project archive you didn't build yourself.
**What to do now:** Run `claude --version` and update if below 2.1.196. Avoid opening untrusted project folders in any coding agent until your vendor ships a patch.

item.title: Your Model Gets the Facts Right but the Format Wrong, or the Format Right but the Facts Wrong — the Two Questions That Tell You Which Problem You Have
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: RAG fixes wrong facts; fine-tuning fixes wrong behavior. The decision tree that keeps most teams from spending three weeks building the wrong solution.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** identify whether your LLM problem is a knowledge problem (reach for RAG) or a behavioral problem (reach for fine-tuning), and know when you need both.
### Three takeaways
- **RAG for facts that change.** If the right answer depends on current docs, tickets, prices, or code, RAG wins by default. Fine-tuning bakes data into weights — it goes stale the moment anything changes. - **Fine-tune for behavior that doesn't.** If the model produces correct information in the wrong format, drifts off a strict JSON schema, or refuses a safe request it should accept — that's behavioral. Retrieval won't fix it. - **Most production apps need both.** RAG keeps knowledge current; fine-tuning disciplines the routes where retrieved answers still aren't in the right shape.
### The decision tree (two questions)
1. **Does the right answer depend on data that changes — pricing, docs, tickets, codebase, policies?** → Start with RAG. 2. **Does the model have correct knowledge but produce it in the wrong format, tone, or structure?** → Fine-tune on the behavioral gap, after RAG is working.
If neither fires, you have a prompting problem. Solve it with prompting before reaching for either approach.
### The catch: retrieval quality sets the ceiling
Evaluating retrieval (with RAGAS or a held-out test set) before fine-tuning is non-optional. A fine-tune on top of poor retrieval teaches the model to hallucinate confidently in your preferred format. Fix retrieval first; fine-tune only on the residual behavioral gap.
### The escalation path in practice
Prompt engineering → add RAG for knowledge gaps → fine-tune for behavioral gaps on RAG-backed routes → re-evaluate retrieval quality after fine-tuning. Each step is reversible until the last.

item.title: Scope Each Subagent to Its Job — Tool Restrictions, Model Overrides, and a Spend Cap in the Claude Agent SDK
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Three AgentDefinition fields — tools, model, and maxBudgetUsd — scope each subagent to exactly what its job needs, prevent accidental writes, and cap spend across the whole query tree.
item.content:encoded:
**A subagent that can't write files can't accidentally overwrite them. Three fields in the Claude Agent SDK's `AgentDefinition` enforce this at the API level, not by convention.**
A subagent defined without a `tools` field inherits every tool the parent has — including `Edit`, `Write`, and `Bash`. For ad hoc use that's fine; in a production pipeline it means a bug in your code-reviewer could rewrite the files it's reviewing. OWASP LLM Top 10 names this pattern "LLM08: Excessive Agency" and recommends minimal tool grants as the primary mitigation. The SDK's `AgentDefinition` implements it directly:
**`tools`** — explicit allowlist, agent can't access anything outside it: ```typescript agents: { "code-reviewer": { description: "Security and quality reviewer for PR diffs.", prompt: "Review for security vulnerabilities and coding standards. Never modify files.", tools: ["Read", "Grep", "Glob"] } } ```
**`model`** — per-subagent model override. Route cheap tasks to `haiku`, complex synthesis to `opus`: ```typescript model: "haiku" // accepts "sonnet", "opus", "fable", a full model ID, or "inherit" ```
**`maxBudgetUsd`** — caps the entire query tree (parent + every spawned subagent) at a dollar amount. The query stops with `error_max_budget_usd` when it hits the limit: ```typescript options: { allowedTools: [..., "Agent"], agents: { ... }, maxBudgetUsd: 5 } ```
Two environment variables bound the tree further: - `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH=1` — prevents subagents from spawning their own (default depth is 3) - `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS=5` — caps parallel execution (default is 20)
**Limit:** `tools`, `model`, and `maxBudgetUsd` are programmatic-definition-only. Filesystem-based agents (`.claude/agents/*.md`) don't support them — they inherit all parent tools. The spend cap requires TypeScript SDK v0.3.219 / Python SDK v0.2.127 or later.
**Why it matters:** tool scope is principle of least privilege applied to agents. A read-only code-reviewer is safe to run in an automated pipeline with broad permissions granted to the parent session — the restriction is enforced by the model layer, not by hoping the agent behaves.

item.title: MCP Config Files Are Leaking Live Credentials — 2,117 Valid Secrets Found, Protocol Gets Stateless Core and Fixed OAuth
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: GitGuardian found 24,008 secrets in public MCP config files (2,117 still valid); the MCP protocol's July update replaces its handshake model with a stateless core and patches an OAuth mix-up attack vector.
item.content:encoded:
**GitGuardian's 2026 secrets-sprawl report found 24,008 secrets in public MCP config files; 2,117 were still valid at time of scan.**
The top exposed types: Google API Keys (19%), PostgreSQL connection strings (14%), Firecrawl API keys (12%). The cause is structural — popular MCP setup guides still recommend pasting API keys directly into JSON config files or command-line arguments, and those configs routinely land on GitHub as dotfiles, project scaffolds, or example repos.
**The one-line fix:** replace hardcoded values with environment variable references. Most MCP clients read these at startup: ```json { "env": { "MY_API_KEY": "${MY_API_KEY}" } } ``` The secret stays in your shell environment; the config file is safe to commit.
**Separately:** the Agentic AI Foundation (Linux Foundation, backed by Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and others) shipped a major protocol update on July 28. Two meaningful changes for server authors: - **Stateless request-centric model:** each request carries all the information it needs; servers no longer maintain per-connection state. This enables load balancing across replicas without shared storage — a real operational improvement for multi-instance deployments. - **Fixed OAuth mix-up attack:** the previous authorization flow let a malicious server intercept authorization codes from a legitimate one. The update closes that with stricter authorization metadata handling.
**Limit:** the stateless shift is a breaking change for servers that rely on connection-level state. The Foundation's deprecation policy keeps old behavior functional for twelve months, so nothing breaks immediately — but migration planning starts now.
**Why it matters:** MCP config files are the new `.env` — they carry real credentials and they need the same secrets-management discipline. The OAuth fix is separately important if you're building servers that authenticate users via third-party providers.

**Four infostealer families now specifically harvest AI coding-agent tokens, MCP config secrets, and prompt histories from developer endpoints.**
Adversa AI's October 2026 catalog documents 10 attack classes against AI coding agents, four targeting predictable local paths without elevated access. The CallbackBeaver family logged 5,000+ samples in a recent 30-day window after expanding to Claude, Cursor, Cline, and Codex targets; [Gurucul's HypeAgent Stealer analysis](https://gurucul.com/blog/hypeagent-stealer-multi-stage-infostealer-hijacking-claude-chatgpt-and-cursor-sessions/) (independent security research) confirms the haul: session and refresh tokens, API keys, full MCP config files with nested credentials, and complete prompt histories. Claude Code's deny rules in `.claude/settings.json` narrow this surface but do not block attacks that execute at the IDE level before the session opens.
**Reduce your exposure now:** - Rotate Claude.ai credentials after opening any untrusted repository - Keep MCP config files free of raw secrets — use env references or a secrets manager - On macOS, exclude `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/` from iCloud backup; the macOS-native Djinn stealer knows this path - Add `.claude/settings.json` deny rules for `git config`, `curl`, and commands that read env files
**Why it matters:** Agent runtimes now hold credentials, code context, and execution capability in one place — infostealers know it, and that directory deserves the same protection as `~/.ssh/`.

item.title: CLAUDE.md Is Layer One — The Other Four Extension Points That Make Claude Code Agents Reliable and Distributable
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code exposes five extension points — CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, subagents, plugins — each solving a different reliability problem. Most teams stop at layer one; here is when to reach for each.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Code's extension stack has five layers: CLAUDE.md anchors always-on context, skills load domain expertise on demand, hooks enforce invariants the model cannot skip, subagents run isolated tasks with separate context windows, and plugins bundle everything into a single distributable unit. Most teams stop at layer one.**
CLAUDE.md works fine for project-level conventions and gotchas — but it has no mechanism for "this rule must hold regardless of what the model decides," no way to isolate a large task from the main context, and no distribution story. The other four layers exist for those gaps.
**Layer 1: CLAUDE.md** — always-on project memory. Everything here is in context for every turn. Keep it short: a long CLAUDE.md fills the context window before the agent starts working. Rule of thumb: if an instruction only matters for one kind of task, it belongs in a skill, not here.
**Layer 2: Skills** (`.claude/skills/`) — on-demand expertise. Only the skill's description is always in context; the body loads only when invoked. A skill that is never triggered costs nothing. Use for: deploy procedures, specialized review checklists, tool-specific workflows. Write one skill per concern, not one giant file.
**Layer 3: Hooks** (`.claude/settings.json`, `hooks:`) — deterministic guardrails. Shell commands that fire before or after tool calls. The model cannot skip or override a hook. Use for invariants: "run lint before every commit", "block API key patterns in diffs". If a rule truly must hold, it belongs in a hook — not in CLAUDE.md, where the model can reason around it.
**Layer 4: Subagents** — isolated context windows. Each subagent starts fresh and can read a large codebase or run a long task without polluting the parent session. Use for: parallel analysis passes, independent code reviews, anything too large to fit in the current context window. Each subagent allocates a full context window; do not spawn one per function.
**Layer 5: Plugins** — distributable bundles. A plugin is a manifest that packages MCP servers, skills, hooks, and commands into a single `claude install` unit. Use when you want to share a workflow across your team or multiple repos without per-project manual configuration.
**The decision rule:** - Know it always → CLAUDE.md - Know it only sometimes → skill - Must be true regardless of the model → hook - Needs its own context window → subagent - Needs to travel with the team → plugin
**Limits:** CLAUDE.md loads only project-scoped context; user-level overrides live at `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Hooks fire on every matching tool call — keep each under ~200ms or they visibly slow the agent loop. Subagents each allocate a full context window; at scale, spawning many gets expensive.
**Sources:** [Context Engineering Beyond CLAUDE.md: The 5-Layer Hierarchy — Pixelmojo](https://www.pixelmojo.io/blogs/context-engineering-ai-coding-agents-beyond-claude-md) · [Dive into Claude Code (arXiv 2604.14228) — VILA-Lab](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.14228v1) · [Claude Code Extension Layer Decision Guide — Hidekazu Konishi](https://hidekazu-konishi.com/entry/claude_code_extension_layers_decision_guide.html)

item.title: GitHub Copilot Adds Scheduled Automations and Agent Merge — Two Modes That Advance a PR Without You Watching
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: GitHub Copilot September releases ship two unattended modes: automations run tasks on hourly/daily/weekly schedules; agent merge handles review feedback, conflict resolution, and CI reruns automatically (preview).
item.content:encoded:
**GitHub Copilot September releases ship two unattended modes: automations run repeatable tasks on a configurable schedule; agent merge takes over once a PR enters review, handling feedback, conflicts, and CI reruns until the branch is green.**
**Automations** are cron jobs for Copilot agent sessions. Define a task (from a template or a custom prompt), pick a cadence — hourly, daily, or weekly — and the agent runs it independently. Use cases GitHub documents: daily dependency audits, weekly stale-branch cleanup, on-demand test generation for changed files. Automations run in Copilot's cloud workspace, not on a local machine.
**Agent merge** takes over once a PR is in review. Enabled per PR, the Copilot agent applies reviewer suggestions, resolves merge conflicts, reruns CI when checks fail, and iterates until the branch is mergeable without you watching the thread at 10pm. The manual cycle it replaces: incorporate feedback → push → wait for CI → handle new conflict from main → repeat.
**Why it matters:** the async PR review cycle is one of the biggest sources of developer context-switching. Offloading the mechanical parts of the review-to-merge loop compounds over a sprint.
**Limits:** agent merge is in preview and stops at design-level disagreements — it will not make architectural decisions or ask for clarification when a reviewer comment is ambiguous. Its interpretation of feedback can diverge from intent. Automations cannot deploy to production or make calls outside GitHub. Both features are currently cloud-only and unavailable in GitHub Enterprise Server.

item.title: Your Vector Index Misses Exact Keywords — Combine BM25 With Vector Search and RRF for a Retriever That Wins Both Ways
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: BM25 finds exact keywords your embedding model misses; combine it with vector ANN and Reciprocal Rank Fusion for a retriever that handles both concept queries and exact strings.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** add a BM25 full-text index alongside your existing vector index and run a single hybrid query that consistently outperforms either retriever alone on real-world question sets with mixed exact-string and concept queries.
**Why either retriever alone fails:** - **Vector search** captures semantic similarity — "bought" and "purchased" score high — but loses exact strings. Ask for "error code E1234" and a dense retriever may return semantically related content that never contains that exact token. - **BM25** scores exact keyword matches using term frequency and document length, with no concept of meaning. "GPT-6.1 Sol" and "the model at one-fifth the price" return different scores even though they describe the same thing. - **Hybrid search** runs both in parallel and merges the ranked lists, covering both failure modes.
**Reciprocal Rank Fusion as the merge function:** RRF computes `1 / (rank + 60)` for each document in each result list, then sums across lists. A document ranked #1 in both lists wins clearly; a document ranked #4 in one list and absent from the other still beats one ranked #30 in each. It requires no calibration and no weight tuning between the two retrievers.
**How to do it in LanceDB (Python):**
```python import lancedb
db = lancedb.connect("rag_db") table = db.open_table("docs")
# One-time: build the BM25 full-text index on the text column table.create_fts_index("text")
# Hybrid query: vector ANN + BM25, fused with RRF results = ( table.search("error code E1234 retry behavior", query_type="hybrid") .rerank(reranker=lancedb.rerankers.RRFReranker()) .limit(5) .to_pandas() ) ```
`create_fts_index` is a one-time call; subsequent queries pick it up automatically. `RRFReranker()` is the default — swap in `CrossEncoderReranker` for a second-pass quality boost at higher latency.
**Three takeaways:** - Hybrid search is the right fix when vector-only RAG handles concept questions well but drops on exact strings, error codes, model IDs, or version numbers. - RRF is parameter-free — no calibration needed between the two retrievers. - LanceDB, Weaviate, and Qdrant expose hybrid search natively; pgvector users need to compose `tsvector` + pgvector queries at the SQL layer — more setup, same principle.
**Limit:** LanceDB's FTS index is disk-backed; for very large tables it adds measurable query latency vs. a pure ANN search. Benchmark with your corpus before deciding whether the quality gain justifies the added query time.
**Sources:** [Hybrid Search in LanceDB: Vector + BM25 + RRF (Python 2026) — YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSGQkyKZ8Rg) · [LanceDB hybrid search docs](https://lancedb.com/docs/search/hybrid-search/) · [Hybrid Search in 100 Lines: BM25 + pgvector with RRF — DEV Community](https://dev.to/gabrielanhaia/hybrid-search-in-100-lines-bm25-pgvector-with-rrf-merge-58cn)

item.title: Your Subagent No Longer Goes Silent When maxTurns Hits — Claude Code 2.1.288 Returns Partial Output and Tells You How to Continue It
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code 2.1.288 fixes two agentic pipeline failure modes: subagents that hit maxTurns now return partial output with a continuation hint, and non-interactive sessions recover from mid-stream API timeouts instead of failing.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Two 2.1.288 fixes — subagents at maxTurns now return partial output with a SendMessage hint, and non-interactive sessions continue from partial responses instead of failing on API timeout.**
If you run agentic pipelines in non-interactive mode — SDK scripts, cloud sessions, CI agents — two fixes in 2.1.288 directly change how failures look.
**1. Subagents reaching maxTurns no longer appear finished.** Previously, a subagent that exhausted its turn budget would return empty or ambiguous output, leaving the orchestrator to infer that it had stopped mid-task. In 2.1.288, the subagent returns its accumulated output marked as `partial`, with a hint: "continue via SendMessage." The orchestrator can inspect the partial result and decide whether to send a follow-up — rather than treating silence as completion.
**2. Mid-stream API timeouts in non-interactive sessions no longer fail the turn.** A dropped connection during a long response previously ended the turn with an error. Now the session retries from the partial response and continues. Thinking-only responses (where the model reasoned but produced no visible output before the disconnect) are retried from scratch. This matters most in cloud sessions and SDK scripts where there's no human to retry.
**3. MCP OAuth scope changes prompt re-authentication automatically.** If an MCP server requests additional OAuth scope mid-session, 2.1.288 now surfaces a re-auth prompt rather than silently failing the tool call.
**4. `/code-review` now accepts `--max-findings <n>` or `--max-findings all`** — useful for CI pipelines that need to control the volume of findings per run.
**What this doesn't fix:** The timeout and partial-response fixes apply only to non-interactive sessions (`-p`, SDK, cloud). Interactive terminal sessions already handled mid-stream failures differently. The maxTurns partial output is a signal to the caller — if your orchestrator doesn't inspect the response body before checking completion status, you won't see the hint.
**Sources:** [Claude Code changelog](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog) · [2.1.288 release notes](https://github.com/Mai0313/claude-code-binaries/releases/tag/2.1.288)

item.title: A Full Fine-Tune Needs 40+ GB of VRAM — QLoRA + Unsloth Shrinks That to a Free Colab T4 in 30 Minutes
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: QLoRA freezes the base model in 4-bit NF4, trains only small LoRA adapters (~1–2% of params), and Unsloth's custom kernels make the whole thing run in ~30 minutes on Colab's free T4 GPU.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: QLoRA freezes the base model in 4-bit, trains only ~1% of params as adapters, and runs on a free T4 in 30 minutes — Unsloth handles the VRAM math.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Fine-tune an open-source model on your own dataset using a free Colab T4 GPU (16 GB), producing a ~50 MB LoRA adapter you can load at inference time or merge with the base weights for a self-contained deployment.
**Three things to know before you start:** - Full fine-tuning a 7B model in bfloat16 requires ~60 GB of VRAM. QLoRA quantizes the frozen base model to 4-bit NF4 (~4 GB for 7B) and only trains the small inserted adapter layers — about 1–2% of total parameters. - [Unsloth](https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth) wraps HuggingFace TRL's SFTTrainer with hand-written CUDA kernels. Unsloth reports 2× faster training and 70% less VRAM than standard HuggingFace; independent results vary by GPU generation — the free T4 (Turing arch) sees less speedup than an A100 (Ampere). - The trained adapter is ~50 MB regardless of base model size. Distribute the adapter alone to HuggingFace Hub, or export merged weights with `save_pretrained_merged()` for a self-contained model file.
**The walkthrough (Qwen 2.5 3B — confirmed on free Colab T4):**
```python # In Colab: Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU, then: pip install "unsloth[colab-new] @ git+https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth.git" pip install --no-deps trl peft accelerate bitsandbytes ```
```python from unsloth import FastLanguageModel
model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained( model_name="unsloth/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct", max_seq_length=2048, load_in_4bit=True, # NF4 quantization — base model frozen )
model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model( model, r=16, # LoRA rank — reliable starting point target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"], lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0, bias="none", ) ```
```python from trl import SFTTrainer from transformers import TrainingArguments
trainer = SFTTrainer( model=model, tokenizer=tokenizer, train_dataset=dataset, # your HuggingFace Dataset dataset_text_field="text", max_seq_length=2048, args=TrainingArguments( per_device_train_batch_size=4, gradient_accumulation_steps=4, num_train_epochs=3, learning_rate=2e-4, fp16=True, output_dir="outputs", ), ) trainer.train()
# Save adapter (~50 MB) or merged weights model.save_pretrained("my-adapter") # model.save_pretrained_merged("my-merged", tokenizer, save_method="merged_16bit") ```
**Where it breaks:** - Models above 8B require at least 24 GB VRAM (A10G or A100 40 GB for 13B+). An 8B model at r=16 uses ~10 GB on the T4. - `max_steps=100` (the tutorial quick-test default) is far too brief for production quality — 500–1000 steps minimum. - `max_seq_length=4096` roughly doubles VRAM requirements relative to 2048. - Free Colab sessions cap at ~12 hours; a 3B run at 1000 steps finishes in time, a larger run may not.
**Full hands-on tutorial with function-calling dataset and complete code:** [LLM_log #015 — Teach a 3B model to call functions with QLoRA + Unsloth on Colab T4](https://datahacker.rs/llm_log-015-fine-tuning-llms-teach-a-3b-model-to-call-functions-with-qlora-unsloth-on-free-colab-t4/).

item.title: Your RAG Answer Cites Nothing — CitationQueryEngine Maps Every Claim to Its Source Chunk
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Two changes to your RAG synthesis step — number every retrieved chunk and instruct the model to cite inline — give every claim a verifiable source. LlamaIndex CitationQueryEngine handles it in 10 lines.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR: Number every retrieved chunk, instruct the model to cite inline, and every RAG answer becomes verifiable — LlamaIndex's CitationQueryEngine handles it in ~10 lines.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** emit numbered inline citations in RAG answers that map each factual claim to the exact source chunk it came from, so answers are verifiable rather than just plausible.
**Three takeaways:** - Every chunk needs a stable anchor — a bracketed number `[1]` injected before the text in the synthesis prompt — for inline citation to work; the model cannot invent a citation it has not seen - `CitationQueryEngine` handles chunk-numbering, prompt injection, and citation parsing in about 10 lines of setup code - A detected citation is not a correct citation — add a structural check (does `[N]` point to a real chunk?) and a semantic check (does chunk N actually support the claim?) before shipping
**The problem with uncited RAG.** Your pipeline retrieves five relevant chunks, sends them to the model, and gets back a fluent answer. The answer is faithful roughly 80% of the time — but you cannot tell which 80%. Without citations, "the model might have hallucinated this" applies to every sentence equally.
**The solution: numbered chunks + prompt instruction.**
```python from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, SimpleDirectoryReader from llama_index.core.query_engine import CitationQueryEngine
docs = SimpleDirectoryReader("./docs").load_data() index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(docs)
query_engine = CitationQueryEngine.from_args( index, similarity_top_k=5, citation_chunk_size=512, # tokens per source node )
response = query_engine.query("What is the refund policy for international orders?") print(response) # "International orders are subject to a 30-day return window [1]. Refunds are # processed within 5 business days of receipt [2]..."
for i, node in enumerate(response.source_nodes, 1): print(f"[{i}] {node.node.text[:120]}...") ```
`CitationQueryEngine` injects numbered chunks into the synthesis prompt and instructs the model to place `[1]`, `[2]`, etc. immediately after any claim derived from that chunk. `response.source_nodes` maps each number back to the original text.
**Manual implementation (any LLM, not just LlamaIndex):**
```python def build_context(chunks): return "\n\n".join(f"[{i+1}] {chunk}" for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks))
system = ( "You are a helpful assistant. Answer using ONLY the provided sources. " "After every factual claim, add [N] where N is the source number you used. " "If a claim is not supported by any source, say so explicitly." )
context = build_context(retrieved_chunks) ```
**Validate citations before you ship.** Two deterministic checks: 1. **Structural**: parse `[N]` markers with `re.findall(r'\[(\d+)\]', response)` and verify all indices are within `range(1, len(chunks)+1)` 2. **Semantic**: check whether the cited chunk contains the claim (fuzzy string match for obvious misses; model-as-judge for subtle ones)
**Limits:** citation density varies — the model sometimes cites the same source repeatedly or omits citations on high-confidence facts. `citation_chunk_size=512` is a reasonable floor; chunks below 100 tokens produce poor synthesis. Citations tell you *which chunk* supported a claim, not whether that chunk is accurate — retrieval quality is still the binding constraint.
**Sources:** [Build RAG with inline citations — LlamaIndex CitationQueryEngine notebook](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/python/examples/workflow/citation_query_engine/) · [RAG_Techniques: citation and groundedness notebooks — NirDiamant/GitHub](https://github.com/NirDiamant/RAG_Techniques) · [Citations in the Key of RAG — cianfrani.dev](https://cianfrani.dev/posts/citations-in-the-key-of-rag/) · [Citation and Grounding: Attributing Answers — neelmishra.github.io](https://neelmishra.github.io/blog/mlops/rag/citation-grounding.html)

item.title: Your OpenAI Client Already Speaks to Together AI — 200+ Open Models, One base_url Change, One ID Format to Learn
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Together AI is OpenAI-compatible across chat, completions, and embeddings. Swap base_url and api_key, learn the org/model-variant ID format, and your existing code runs Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, and 200+ others.
item.content:encoded:
**Your existing OpenAI client reaches Llama 3.3, Qwen3, DeepSeek, and 200+ other open models by changing base_url and api_key — the only integration difference is Together AI's org/model-variant ID format.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Run any of Together AI's 200+ open-source models from your existing OpenAI SDK with two environment variable changes - Look up model IDs in the catalog before writing code against them - Prototype on serverless endpoints and move to dedicated endpoints without changing any other code
**Three things to take away:** - Together AI's API is OpenAI-compatible across chat, completions, vision, embeddings, and TTS — `base_url` and `api_key` are the only changes - Model IDs use `org/model-variant` format: `meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-Turbo`, not `llama-3.3-70b` — this is what breaks most integrations - Serverless and dedicated endpoints share the same API surface — switch by pointing at the dedicated endpoint URL, nothing else changes in your code
**Walk-through:**
```python # Before: your existing OpenAI code from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() # uses OPENAI_API_KEY
# After: Together AI — same SDK, different target import os from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI( api_key=os.environ["TOGETHER_API_KEY"], base_url="https://api.together.xyz/v1" ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-Turbo", # not "llama-3.3-70b" messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}], max_tokens=512, ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ```
Or use the native Together SDK: `pip install together`, then `from together import Together; client = Together()` with the same model IDs.
**Finding model IDs:** check [docs.together.ai/docs/serverless/models](https://docs.together.ai/docs/serverless/models) or call `client.models.list()`. The catalog covers Llama 3.3, Qwen3, DeepSeek V4 series, Mixtral, and code-specialized variants.
**What Together AI adds beyond Fireworks:** built-in fine-tuning (upload JSONL, launch a run, the result is a deployable endpoint on the same API), batch processing at up to 50% lower per-token cost for offline workloads (Together AI's own figure), and a wider catalog including image and video generation.
**Real limits:** - Model IDs don't map from OpenAI names — there's no automatic translation; always check the catalog before writing code against a model name - Together AI claims 2.75x faster serverless inference than competitors per their own benchmarks — independent head-to-head data is limited, test your own latency requirements before committing - Serverless can throttle under high load; dedicated endpoints are fixed-price (per GPU-hour, model-dependent) and require upfront volume estimates - Context window and rate limits vary by model — don't assume they match OpenAI's, check the model card for each
**Sources:** [OpenAI compatibility — Together AI docs](https://docs.together.ai/docs/inference/openai-compatibility) · [Available models — Together AI docs](https://docs.together.ai/docs/serverless/models) · [Open Source AI Inference API w/ Together — YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_GQfj3jhXVM) · [Together AI: Serverless GPU inference guide — Zaira Labs](https://zairalabs.ai/guide/tools/together-ai/)

item.title: Your Two Claude Code Sessions Can Now Message Each Other — Mention the Target With `@` and Claude Routes the Handoff
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Cross-session messaging (v2.1.224+) lets one Claude Code session warn another about a breaking change or hand off a decision — text only, works on the same machine with no extra setup.
item.content:encoded:
**Cross-session messaging lets one Claude Code session warn another about a breaking change or send a decision across — useful for parallel worktrees or a frontend/backend split, with no relay from you.**
When you run a library in one terminal and a consuming app in another, the usual workflow is: make a change in session A, then manually re-explain it in session B. Cross-session messaging (v2.1.224+, macOS and Linux) removes that relay.
**How it works.** Claude uses two tools under the hood — `ListAgents` to discover your other live sessions and `SendMessage` to write to one. You never call either directly. Ask Claude to pass something and it handles the addressing:
``` Let the payments-api session know that users.name is now users.display_name ```
To name a specific target, type `@` followed by the session name — Claude Code autocompletes from the live session list. For names with spaces: `@"release notes"`.
**`/list-agents`** shows what Claude can reach: subagents, your other sessions on this machine, and (when connected to Remote Control) cloud sessions and sessions on other machines.
**Useful patterns:** - **Parallel worktrees on the same repo:** each session notifies the other when a shared API contract changes. - **Monorepo frontend/API split:** the API session sends "schema migration finished" instead of you watching two terminals.
**Wait-for-idle:** ask Claude to notify you when a long task finishes: ``` Tell me when the migration session finishes what it's working on ``` Claude subscribes; the other session sends one notice when it next goes idle.
**What crosses: text only.** Not conversation history, not files, not permissions. The receiving session's own permission rules still apply to anything the message asks for. A received message can never answer a permission prompt on your behalf or change project configuration.
**Limits:** same-machine only without Remote Control; ~1 million character message cap; rapid bursts to one session are rate-limited automatically; macOS and Linux only for same-machine (native Windows requires v2.1.234+).
**Sources:** [Cross-session messaging — Claude Code docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging) · [Week 32 digest — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/whats-new/2026-w32) · [Claude Code cross-session communication — nexforce.ai](https://nexforce.ai/en/blog/claude-code-sessions-communicate-mid-task)

**VS Code 1.140 (released September 30) turns on HydraFusion multi-model routing by default in Copilot chat and adds experimental multi-folder agent sessions that isolate agent work across separate repos.**
**HydraFusion** is now on by default in VS Code's Copilot chat. It automatically routes each coding task across three execution patterns: route to a single model directly, cascade from a cheaper model to a stronger one when quality gates aren't met, or have a second model critique and revise the first's output. GitHub's own benchmarks claim 67% cost reduction vs Claude Opus 5 at matched quality on TerminalBench 2.1 — those numbers are GitHub's, independent benchmarks pending. It remains a research preview and its behavior may change.
**Multi-folder agent sessions (experimental)** let each chat tab own its own folder, branch, and PR. Agent work on repo A cannot contaminate repo B in the same VS Code window. Useful for managing related but separate services or packages without leaking context between sessions.
**Worktree symlink reuse:** the new `git.worktreeSymlinkFolders` setting symlinks `node_modules` (and other directories listed in `.gitignore`) from the main checkout into each new worktree. This cuts worktree setup time from "full install" to "symlink creation" on repos with heavy dependencies.
**Limits:** HydraFusion is still a research preview — intermediate model drafts are hidden until completion, and the routing rules may change. Multi-folder sessions are experimental and may not persist across restarts.
**Why it matters:** HydraFusion's cascade pattern (try a cheaper model, escalate only if a quality gate fails) is a practical design principle for anyone building multi-model routing in their own agent stack — regardless of whether you use VS Code Copilot.

item.title: The Claude Design Export Is a Bundle — What's in the ZIP, How Claude Code Reads It, and Where Drift Starts
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: The Claude Design "Handoff to Claude Code" export packages components, tokens, and a target-stack README into a bundle Claude Code reads as a spec — drift starts the moment you edit generated code without returning to the canvas.
item.content:encoded:
**"Handoff to Claude Code" packages your Claude Design project into a bundle — components, design tokens, layout, and a README — that Claude Code reads as a spec. Drift starts the moment you edit generated code without returning to the canvas.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** export a Claude Design project as a handoff bundle, load it into a Claude Code session, and know the decision rule for "iterate here vs. return to the canvas."
**Three things to know before you start:**
1. The bundle contains the component HTML/CSS/JS, the design tokens used on the canvas, a layout spec, and a README that tells Claude Code the target stack and conventions. Claude Code reads the README first and works from the spec rather than guessing from the visual output. 2. Drift between the design and the code begins the first time you edit generated code without going back to the canvas to make the change there. The fix is to return to Claude Design and re-export; trying to manually reconcile grows exponentially with each round. 3. The reverse trip already exists: `/design` in Claude Code reads your repo's existing tokens before drawing. Use it when you want to bring something already-coded back into the design surface for a new direction — it starts from your system, not from scratch.
**Concrete walkthrough:**
1. Complete your prototype in Claude Design. Before exporting, test empty states, error states, and varying data volumes — these are the scenarios the bundle consistently misses. Revise on canvas now. 2. Select **Export → Handoff to Claude Code**. Choose **Local agent** (for a terminal session) or **Web session** (for claude.ai). Claude Design generates a one-line command to paste. 3. Paste the command into a new Claude Code session. Claude fetches the bundle, reads the README, and generates components following the spec. 4. If the inferred stack is wrong (the README defaults to React/Tailwind unless your codebase is linked), re-open the Claude Design chat, note your target stack explicitly, and re-export. 5. For subsequent changes: revise on the Claude Design canvas, re-export, paste the new command. Editing generated code directly is fine for one-offs, but breaks the sync for anything you want to keep in step with the design.
**Limits:** The bundle URL expires — share it before collaborating with teammates. Linking a full monorepo causes browser lag in Claude Design; attach only the package or directory containing your relevant components. Inline comments added in Claude Design may not survive saves; paste them into the canvas chat instead.

item.title: `--output-format stream-json` Turns a Long Claude Code Run Into a Live NDJSON Feed Your Pipeline Can Act On
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: stream-json emits one NDJSON event per step as Claude runs — pipe through jq to watch tool calls, capture cost, and trigger conditional pipeline steps without waiting for the final result.
item.content:encoded:
**`--output-format stream-json` turns a long Claude Code run into a live NDJSON feed — pipe it through `tee` and `jq` to observe what's happening and extract cost or tool-call counts before the run finishes.**
Claude Code's `-p` (print) mode has three output formats:
- `text` — human-readable default; great for terminals, useless for scripts - `json` — one JSON envelope after the run finishes: `{type, result, cost_usd, duration_ms, usage}` - `stream-json` — NDJSON events emitted as the run progresses, one event per step
Use `json` for simple one-shot queries where you only need the final answer. Use `stream-json` when the run is long and you want observability: log individual tool calls, surface progress to a dashboard, or trigger downstream steps without polling.
**Workflow: capture and parse in parallel**
```bash # Run the task and write every event to a log; watch live at the same time claude -p "Review the last 5 commits and list files touched" --output-format stream-json --verbose | tee /tmp/claude-run.ndjson
# After the run: extract cost and token usage from the final result event jq -rs 'last | {cost_usd, duration_ms, usage}' /tmp/claude-run.ndjson
# Count how many individual tool calls fired jq -rs '[.[] | select(.type == "tool")] | length' /tmp/claude-run.ndjson ```
Add `--verbose` to include tool-call events with the tool name, input arguments, and output. Without it, you get turn-level events but not the details of what each tool did.
**When to reach for it over `json`:** stream-json is worthwhile when the run takes more than a few seconds and you want CI logs that show what Claude actually did — not just the final answer. For quick one-shot prompts, `json` is simpler and produces a single parseable line.
**Limits:** The NDJSON event schema is versioned; check the [`--output-format` reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference) before treating specific field names as stable across CLI versions. The `jq` selects above use field names consistent with current releases but may need updating after major CLI upgrades.
